question.text: When computing free-float market capitalisation for a value-weighted index like the Nifty 50 or BSE Sensex (used by Aravalli Long-Short Fund as a hedge benchmark), which ONE of the following categories of shareholding is INCLUDED in free float (i.e., NOT excluded)?

answer.text: Shares held by founders / directors / acquirers with control element
Shares held by the Government as promoter / acquirer
Free-floating shares held by mutual funds, insurance companies, retail and other public investors
Locked-in shares that cannot be sold in the open market in normal course

explanation.text: The Logic: Per Box 8.2 ('Concept of Free Float'), free float EXCLUDES: promoter/founder/director holdings with control intent, government promoter stakes, FDI-route holdings, strategic private-body stakes, associate/cross-holdings, employee welfare trusts, and locked-in shares. It INCLUDES non-strategic holdings — including those held by mutual funds, insurers, retail and public investors — which represent genuinely available-for-trading shares. The Trap: Options A, B, and D are all on the EXCLUSION list. Only Option C represents genuinely floating shares that determine index weight. Cross-Exam Context: XXI-B (PM) and XV (RA) test free-float methodology. XIX-C / XIX-D cover it for AIF benchmarking. BSE Sensex moved to free-float on 1-Sept-2003; Nifty 50 on 26-June-2009. Manager's Pro-Tip: If you are designing a Cat III pair-trade against a large-cap with a newly-unlocked promoter stake, remember the index free-float weight will re-base UP once the lock-in expires — index funds and ETFs must buy proportionally, creating a short-lived technical bid. Time your short leg entry carefully around free-float reconstitution dates.
